standard.title: First Nations visual arts continuing and revitalising cultures
standard.description: explore ways that First Nations Australians use visual arts to continue and revitalise cultures
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored how First Nations Australians use visual arts to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place (AC9AVA4E02). They can identify cultural symbols and understand that arts serve community functions. They have not yet examined how First Nations arts serve as active cultural continuation and revitalisation, or explored contemporary applications such as street art, popular culture and textiles.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore ways that First Nations Australians use visual arts to continue and revitalise cultures — examining the range of purposes, forms and contexts in which this occurs.

nodes.label: Multiple purposes of First Nations visual arts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain that First Nations Australian visual arts serve multiple purposes — cultural practice, narrative, identity declaration, community communication and cultural revitalisation.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different purposes of one First Nations Australian artwork (e.g. cultural practice and narrative, or community communication and identity).
nodes.typical_width: Explore how First Nations Australian artworks may have multiple purposes simultaneously; use Viewpoints questions to interrogate what each work is doing and for whom; discuss the difference between art as cultural practice and art as revitalisation.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian artists embed themselves and their communities in artworks in diverse forms — explore representations of First Nations Australians as superheroes in comics and popular culture
Explore how visual arts created by First Nations Australians communicate cultural knowledge to the broader community through textiles, fashion and applied design
nodes.hinge_reason: The multiple-purposes concept is new at Y5-6 — students who understand only 'connection to Country/Place' from Y3-4 are not equipped to engage with the full range of functions the descriptor requires, including revitalisation as an active, ongoing practice.

response_modes.reason: The concept of revitalisation — arts actively continuing and renewing culture — needs explicit introduction. Students often assume arts only document culture; discussion prompts help them see arts as a living, forward-looking practice.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two different purposes of a First Nations Australian artwork
Explains the difference between arts as cultural practice and arts as cultural revitalisation

nodes.label: Contemporary forms and contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate a range of contemporary First Nations Australian visual arts forms — site-specific work, street art, murals, installation, textiles — and explore how they communicate and celebrate cultural knowledge.
nodes.minimum_width: Explore one contemporary First Nations Australian artwork in a non-gallery form (street art, mural, installation, textile); identify how it communicates cultural knowledge.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate a range of site-specific artworks, murals, street art and installations by First Nations Australian artists; explore how these forms communicate cultural knowledge; use Viewpoints questions to deepen questioning; investigate meaning and purpose.
wider: Investigate site-specific artworks by First Nations Australian artists — explore how the site itself shapes the meaning of the work and how placement communicates cultural significance
Investigate how First Nations Australian artists use fashion and textiles to share cultural knowledge with the broader community — examine specific visual conventions used

response_modes.reason: Students who are only exposed to gallery-based or historical First Nations Australian artworks develop an incomplete picture of how these arts function. Contemporary forms — street art, textiles, popular culture — show that cultural revitalisation is ongoing.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of contemporary First Nations Australian arts forms (street art, murals, fashion, superhero comics) is genuinely diverse and unexpected — students who engage with this range substantially revise their understanding of what First Nations visual arts look like today.
success_criteria: Explores at least one contemporary First Nations Australian artwork in a non-gallery form
Identifies how it communicates cultural knowledge or identity

nodes.label: Identity, resilience and storytelling
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how First Nations Australian artists embed identity, storytelling and resilience in artworks as a visual declaration — across a diverse range of forms and contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how one First Nations Australian artwork serves as a declaration of identity, storytelling or resilience.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how diverse First Nations Australian artists embed identity, storytelling and resilience across multiple forms; investigate how visual conventions carry cultural messages; discuss what cultural continuation and revitalisation mean in practice.
wider: Compare how First Nations Australian artists in different contemporary forms (gallery, public, fashion, popular culture) use similar visual conventions to communicate the same cultural messages
Use Viewpoints questions to investigate what you already know, what you need to learn, and what questions you would ask a First Nations Australian artist about their practice and community

response_modes.reason: Students bring together their understanding of multiple purposes, contemporary forms and the concept of revitalisation to reach the full descriptor demand: First Nations visual arts as an ongoing, living practice of cultural continuation.

success_criteria: Explains how at least one First Nations Australian artwork serves as a declaration of identity, storytelling or resilience
Uses language that reflects understanding of arts as active cultural revitalisation — not only preservation
